title: Guess Which Marathon Our Data Got Right | Terra
summary: We matched 532 Terra users across three marathons against 65,000 official finishers. In Berlin, our sample was 26 minutes faster with nearly three times the…
body_markdown:
## How I pulled the users


I run a mass-start detector on the Terra database. It looks for unusual numbers of distinct users starting within a few kilometres of each other, on a day that does not usually look like that. For someone to land in an event bucket they have to start near the start line, near the start time, and then run close to the advertised distance. Then I clean a bit, so a parkrun that wandered through the same coordinates does not sneak in.


The filter is defensible. I can be pretty confident they ran the event I think they ran. What is not obvious is who is missing. These users wear a connected device, sync to a Terra-connected app, record GPS, and look like they finished the distance. That is not everyone who finished.


Berlin was 27 September. KL Standard Chartered was 4 October. Intercare Blouberg was 3 October.


## Berlin


Official field, Mika Timing chip times: 50,012 finishers. Median 4:11:19. 7.47% under three hours. Winner 2:02:50.


Terra: 267 users. Median 3:45. 19.9% under three hours. One user in the 2:15–2:20 band. About seventy percent COROS.


Coverage is half a percent. The sample is 26 minutes faster than the field and almost three times as likely to break three hours.


Two hundred and sixty-seven is a large sample. Unfortunately it is large enough to be sure about the wrong race. If you published “Berlin 2026 from wearables” from this, you would describe a faster, more serious amateur race than the one that happened.


Why? Everyone in the Terra sample uses a wearable. Not everyone in a city marathon does. The people who sync to us are probably more active, and more likely to have travelled for a destination marathon. Nothing in the sample tells you that. The official list does.


## Blouberg


Official field, Mobii Elite: 2,508 finishers. Median 4:40:38. 1.48% sub-3. Winner 2:35:36.


Terra: 99 users. Median 4:35. 1.0% sub-3. One user in the 2:55–3:00 band. About seventy-two percent Garmin.


Coverage is about 4%. The medians are close. The sub-3 rates are very similar. We still miss the very sharp end of the club athletes, but the pack is the pack.


Why does this one work? It is a Comrades / Two Oceans qualifier. Local Garmin club culture happens to look like Terra’s South African base. Selection into the database looks like selection into the race. That is luck!


## Kuala Lumpur


I cannot get the full 2026 results. The organiser posts them as a lookup, so I cannot compute a field median. I can see the podiums, and I can see 2024.


In 2024 the two mass Malaysian men’s categories were 8,046 finishers, medians 5:40 and 5:45. International open categories were faster and much smaller. Known sub-3s were about 0.4%. This year’s winners were 2:21 and 2:39. Hot, humid, slow. That part makes sense.


Terra 2026: 166 users. Median 5:13. Zero sub-3. Two users in the 3:10–3:15 band, nobody faster. Almost all COROS. Coverage 1.28%, though that is against 12,964 participants rather than finishers.


Against that prior, 5:13 is about 30 minutes faster than the Malaysian mass, and in line with 2024 Open men. The prior only covers Malaysian men, while our users probably include women and international runners, so treat this as a rough comparison rather than a like-for-like one. This year’s winner was slower than 2024 (2:21 vs 2:18). If the field slowed with the elite, Terra looks more biased, not less.

## How can I tell if the sample matches the field?


The usual way to test this is to treat the official file as the population, and ask whether our times could have been a random draw from it.


We normally use two tests for this. A chi-square goodness-of-fit test asks whether Terra users land in each time band at the same rate as the field. A Kolmogorov–Smirnov test looks at the whole curve: the biggest gap between the two cumulative distributions. For one given value, such as the share under three hours, a binomial test against the official proportion is enough. A t-test is the wrong tool here.


The times are not normally distributed, and a t-test only asks “are they faster on average?”, which is a narrower question than “does this sample look like the field?” A non-significant p-value does not prove the sample is the field; it means a sample this size did not detect a difference. The other trap is precision. A big sample gives a tight estimate and a confident answer, but only about the people in it. Berlin’s n is big enough to be sure, and still wrong. Berlin fails every test, and Blouberg passes them.


### **The sampling traps I need to look out for**


**1. n looks like a population.**


Two hundred finishers feels like “enough.” Enough for what? Enough to estimate *this sample’s* median. Not enough to stand in for 50,000 other people (they did not sync a GPS watch we can see). Representativeness is not a sample size. It is a statement about who is missing.


**2. The same filter, different bias.**


Berlin and Blouberg data were selected in an identical way. The bias changed anyway. A pipeline that is “fair” across races is not unbiased across races. Fairness of method is not fairness of sample. The device mix is a clue: about seventy percent COROS in Berlin and almost all COROS in KL, but about seventy-two percent Garmin in Blouberg. Different devices, different communities, different selection.


**3. Comparing samples as if they were races.**


Terra Berlin 3:45 versus Terra KL 5:13 is a real contrast in *our users* . It's not just Berlin versus Kuala Lumpur; the actual users are probably very different, and the event and conditions (and many other factors) may also differ, but we can’t make assumptions about any of them.


**4. Treating gaps in our data as a finding.**


KL Terra has zero sub-3s. The published podiums are full of times we do not have. Absence in the warehouse is not absence on the course. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.


**5. Being sure.**


Berlin’s Terra median is not noisy. That is the trap. Selection bias does not widen your error bars. You can get a tight estimate of the wrong population and call it science.


### **What about your watch?**


Every “you’re faster than 70% of runners” badge hides the same question. 70% of whom?


If the comparison is with other people who wear the same device and sync their runs, you are being ranked against something that could look more like the Terra Berlin sample than the whole Berlin field. That group is probably fitter and keener than the person next to you on the start line.


It isn’t all bad news. If that group is faster than the real field, your percentile is probably lower than it would be in the actual race. Your watch might be underselling you!


So next time an app tells you where you rank, ask who it is comparing you with. If the answer is “people who own this watch”, that is a real number. It just isn’t the same as “runners.”
